in  thy  seed  shall  all  the  nations  of  the  earth  be

Such  too  was  the  faith  by  which  Abel  and  Enoch, 
Noah  and  Moses,  the  patriarchs  and  the  prophets, 
pleased  God.  "  By  faith"  the  elders  obtained  a 
good  report ;  yet  S.  Paul  speaks  throughout  of 
nothing  but  deeds  of  faith.  "  By  faith,"  says  S. 
Paul,  one  after  another  of  that  goodly  'army,  they

"wrought  righteousness."  By  deeds  of  faith,  did 
"  Noah  become  heir  of  the  righteousness  which  is 
by  faith."  A  deed  of  faith  "  was  counted  to  Phine- 
has  for  righteousness  unto  all  generations,  for  ever- 
more0," i.  e.  not  only  for  this  world,  but  also  for  the 
world  to  come.  By  a  deed  of  faith  was  "  Rahab  the 
harlot,"  S.James  says,  " justified"1."  She  had  not 
repented  when  the  spies  came ;  for  Scripture  says, 
"they  came  into  a  harlot's  house,  named  Rahab6." 
She  believed  before :  ' '  The  Lord  your  God,  He  is

God  converted  her  through  the  coming  of  the

the  messengers  and  sent  them  out  another  way." 

Faith  and  works  are  one  compound  whole,  even 
as  in  man,  in  whom  they  exist,  body  and  soul  are 
one  living  man.  Faith  is  first  in  order  of  relation  ;

but  since,  as  our  Lord  says,  the  purpose  of  the 
heart  is  an  inward  act,  faith  is  not  for  a  moment 
separate  from  action.  S.  Paul's  "  Who  art  Thou, 
Lord?"  was  followed  up  at  once  with  "  Lord,  what 
wilt  Thou  have  me  to  do  ?"  His  whole  life  of  toil 
and  suffering  lay,  in  purpose,  in  that  first  confession 
of  his  faith.  His  faith,  his  love,  his  devotedness 
entered  into  his  soul  in  one. 

Faith  and  deeds  of  faith  are,  both  of  them,  graces 
of  this  passing  world.  Yet  God  hath  appointed 
that  not  only  shall  they  be  inseparable,  but  that 
they  shall  strengthen  one  another.  "  Faith,"  S. 
James  says,  "  wrought  with  or  co-operated  with 
(crvvrjpytC)  Abraham's  works,  and  by  works  was 
faith  made  perfect"  (ertAetco^) .  S.  James  like  S. 
Paul  speaks  of  faith  as  the  root ;  "  faith  co-operated 
with  his  works."  Faith  made  them  what  they  be- 
came, "  pleasing  and  acceptable  to  God."  But  the 
works  re-acted  on  the  faith,  and  "  made  it  perfect." 
God  has  so  made  us,  that  acts  are  the  great  means 
of  influencing  our  inward  minds.  Thoughts  and 
feelings,  of  themselves,  die  away  ;  words,  the  more 
evaporate  them  ;  acts  concentrate  and  give  them  an 
intensity  of  strength.  To  act  lovingly  increases 
love,  softens  unlove ;  to  act  trustfully,  increases 
trust ;  to  act  suspiciously,  aggravates  suspicion  ; 
to  act  unkindly,  embitters  the  unkindness.  Acts 
strengthen  the  inward  feeling,  both  because,  on  the 
neglect  or  the  use  of  the  grace  of  God,  God  with- 
draws or  increases  His  grace  ;  and  because,  our  life 


30 

here  being  in  action  and  duty,  God  has  seen  good 
so  to  act  upon  our  souls  for  good,  so  to  allow  us  to 
act  upon  our  own  souls  for  evil.  But  for  good  or  for 
evil,  man,  through  his  own  choice,  does  most  ener- 
getically stamp  the  character  of  his  acts  upon  his 
soul.  Faith  grows  with  deeds  of  faith.  Faith  is  the 
root  of  the  living  tree ;  through  faith,  as  the  root, 
the  mustard  seed  grows  and  becometh  a  tree  :  faith 
draws  in  nourishment  to  it  from  the  dew  of  heaven, 
and  twines  around  the  rifted  Rock;  but  with  the 
growth  of  the  tree,  the  root  itself  grows.  So  faith 
from  first  to  last  unites  us  to  our  Lord  ;  faith  is  the 
channel  of  every  grace  to  the  soul ;  yet  faith  itself 
is  strengthened  by  the  very  acts  of  which  it  is  the 
spring. 

God  teaches  us  this  in  that  great  pattern  of  faith, 
the  type  of  the  Church,  the  father  of  the  faithful. 
His  life  is  a  succession  of  trials  of  faith,  mounting 
and  rising  above  one  another',  until  they  close  in

him  for  righteousness,  and  he  was  called  the  friend 
of  God."  Abraham  was  already  justified  before  the 
faith,  of  which  Moses  and  S.  Paul  say,  "it  was 
imputed  to  him  for  righteousness."  For  this  was 
said  of  the  promise  of  a  son ;  but  Abraham  had 
already  believed  and  obeyed  before  this  promise, 
and  God  had  already  said  to  him,  "  I  will  bless  thee, 

f  Gen.  xiv.  22  ;  xiii.  13. 


32 

and  thou  shalt  be  a  blessing,  and  in  thee  shall  the 
families  of  the  earth  be  blessed."  But  with  the  in- 
crease of  trials  of  faith,  there  was  an  increase  of 
faith  ;  and  with  the  increase  of  faith,  there  was  an 
increase  of  righteousness. 

So  then,  S.  Paul,  when  he  says,  "  it  was  imputed 
to  him  for  righteousness,"  as  well  as  S.  James,  when 
he  says,  that  those  words  were  fulfilled  in  him, 
speaks  not  of  Abraham's  first  being  received  to 
righteousness,  but  of  the  increase  of  righteousness. 
Both  lay  down  general  principles  ;  S.  Paul,  that 
faith  is  ever,  first  and  last,  the  root  of  our  justifica- 
tion ;  S.  James,  that  that  faith  justifieth  not,  which 
does  not,  when  it  is  possible,  issue  in  act.  But 
since  Abraham  was  already  justified,  then  S.  Paul, 
when  he  says  that  "  faith  was  counted  to  him  for 
righteousness,"  does  not  mean  that  it  was  accounted 
to  him,  as  being  what  it  was  not.  It  was  accounted 
to  him,  not  on  account  of  any  previous  desert,  but 
in  itself.  God,  of  His  own  free  grace,  so  counted 
it  to  him ;  yet  as  the  faith  was  inward,  so  was  the 
righteousness  which  accrued  to  him.  The  righte- 
ousness of  which  S.  Paul  too  speaks,  is  an  accession 
of  righteousness  upon  an  accession  of  faith ;  as  in 
the  Gospels  it  is  said  of  our  Lord's  disciples,  "His 
disciples  believed  on  Him,"  i.  e.,  they  received  a 
further  degree  of  belief  to  which  their  former  belief 
was,  as  it  were,  no  belief.  To  the  mere  character 
of  "  being  pardoned"  there  is  no  accession,  there 
are  no  degrees.  But  S.  Paul,  as  well  as  S.  James, 


33 

speaks  of  a  righteousness,  of  which  there  are  de- 
grees, a  store  which  is  being  continually  enlarged, 
as  God  accounts  for  righteousness  the  gift  and  grace 
of  faith,  which  He  first  imparts  and  afterwards 
elicits  and  enlarges. 

When  on  the  other  hand,  S.  James  says,  that 
"  the   Scripture  was  fulfilled,"  he,  in  fact,  asserts 
the  identity  of  that  living  faith  of  which  S.  Paul 
speaks,  with  the  works  of  faith  of  which  he  himself 
is  speaking.      The   Scripture  "  Abraham  believed 
God,  and  it  was  accounted  to  him  for  righteous- 
ness," received  a  renewed  and  enlarged  fulfilment 
by  his  being  justified  through  the  offering  of  his 
son.     Yet  this  could  not  have  been,  had  there  not 
been  the  same  principle  of  both  ;  faith,  not  issuing 
as  yet  in  act,  when,  as  in  believing  the  promise  of 
the  son,  there  was  no  outward  act  to  perform  ;  and 
faith  issuing  in  act,  so  soon  as  God  called  it  to  act, 
as  in  the  sacrifice  of  that  son.     Nor  could  it  again 
have  been  a  fulfilment,  unless  the  result  had  been 
the  same,  and  S.  Paul's  words  "  counted  unto  him 
for  righteousness,"  had  been  the  same  as  James's 
"  were  justified."    His  faith  was  the  channel  to  him 
of  real  righteousness,  and  since  Abraham  was  al- 
ready justified,  he  through  that  living  faith,  a  faith, 
when  it  could,  "  working  by  love,"  received  an  ac- 
cession to  that  righteousness11. 

h  S.  Paul,  when  he  excludes  works  from  justification,  plainly  ex- 
cludes all  works,  done  before  grace,  whether  ceremonial  or  moral.  He 
himself  explains,  that  under  "  the  deeds  of  the  law,"  he  includes  the

'34 

iii.  And  so  also  as  to  the  relation  of  good  works  to 
eternal  life.  Those  on  the  one  side,  may  be  mainly 
anxious  to  shew  that  our  good  works  have  of  them- 
selves no  proper  claim  to  eternal  life,  and  so  they 
wish  to  set  forth  the  free  mercy  and  goodness  of  God 
in  Christ,  Who  "  crowneth  in  mercy  and  loving- 
kindness,"  all  those  whose  "  sins  He  has  forgiven  and 
healed  all  their  infirmities."  Those  on  the  other  side, 
may  chiefly  intend  to  secure  the  literal  meaning  of 
Holy  Scripture,  when  it  speaks  of  reward,  that  "God 
will  render  unto  every  man  according  to  his  works1 ;" 

moral  law.  For,  as  the  very  ground  of  his  words,  "  by  the  deeds  of  the 
law  there  shall  no  flesh  be  justified  in  His  sight,"  he  subjoins,  "for  by 
the  law  is  the  knowledge  of  sin."  (Rom.  iii.  20.)  But  he  himself  ex- 
plains this  of  the  decalogue,  "  I  had  not  known  sin,  but  by  the  law  ; 
for  I  had  not  known  lust,  except  the  law  had  said,  '  Thou  shalt  not 
covet.' "  (Ibid.,  vii.  7.)  S.  James,  on  the  other  hand,  plainly  means, 
works  which  follow  immediately  upon  justification,  as  appears  from 
his  •  instancing  Rahab.  Yet  he  speaks  also  of  works  as  having  the 
same  relation  to  Rahab's  faith,  who  was  just  converted,  as  to  Abra- 
ham's in  the  crowning  act  of  the  living  operative  faith  of  half  a  cen- 
tury. S.  Paul  says  that  a  man  is  justified  by  faith  without  works, 
preceding  faith,  yet  by  a  faith  which  worketh  by  love.  S.  James 
denies  that  a  man  is  justified  by  a  faith  which  worketh  not.  The 
statements  of  the  two  Apostles  are  correlative.  S.  James's  words  do 
not  exclude  the  need  of  God's  mercy,  as  appears  from  his  words,  just 
before,  "  He  shall  have  judgment  without  mercy,  that  hath  shewed  no 
mercy  ;  and  mercy  rejoiceth  against  judgment"  (ii.  13)  ;  and  S.  Paul 
teaches  explicitly  the  same  as  S.  James  when  he  says,  "  The  doers  of 
the  law  shall  be  justified,"  i.  e.  they  who  by  the  grace  of  God  obey 
Him,-  as  our  Lord  says,  "  If  ye  love  Me,  keep  My  commandments." 
And  again,  "  In  Christ  Jesus  neither  circumcision  availeth  any  thing, 
nor  uncircurncision,  but  faith  which  worketh  by  love."  This  harmony 
of  S.  Paul  and  S.  James  is  given  by  S.  Augustine  with  his  usual  clear- 
ness. See  note  at  the  end.

thou  shouldest  praise  God  Himself  for  ever.  O 
forget  not  all  His  benefits  if  thou  wouldest  that 
thy  soul  should  bless  the  Lord  Who  crowneth  thee 
in  mercy  and  loving  kindness0."  "  The  Lord  shall 
rejoice  in  His  works,  not  in  thine  as  though  thine ; 
for  thy  works  too,  if  evil,  are  so  through  thine  ini- 
quity; if  good,  through  the  grace  of  Godd." 

It  is  easy  to  select  hard  and  technical  sayings  on 

c  In  Ps.  cii.  §  7.  d  Id.  in  Ps.  ciii.  Serm.  iv.  §  15.

the  one  side  and  on  the  other ;  it  is  easy  to  find 
sayings  which  deny  the  value  of  works  wrought 
through  the  grace  of  Christ,  or  which  exaggerate 
them.  It  is  easy  to  misunderstand,  hard  to  under- 
stand unless  we  love.  For  unless  we  love,  we  do  not 
wish  to  understand.  It  is  easy  to  distort,  hard 
to  see  aright,  unless  we  wish  to  see  one  another 
and  one  another's  meaning,  in  the  light  and  truth 
and  love  of  God. 

All  believe  that  Christ  is  the  Way,  the  Truth,  and 
the  Life,  Himself  the  Way,  to  Himself  the  Life.  All 
believe  that  to  do,  by  His  grace,  the  works  which 
He  giveth  and  willeth  us  to  do,  is  the  way  by  which 
we  hold  on  in  that  Way.  He  Alone  is  "  the  cause 
of  our  reigning6 ;"  "  deeds"  done  by  His  grace,  are 
the  "way  to"  His  eternal  "kingdom;"  yet  we 
should  not  have  been  in  the  way,  had  not  He  freel} 
placed  us  in  it ;  we  should  fail  by  the  way,  unless 
He  through  His  grace  strengthened  us ;  we  should 
perish  from  the  way,  unless  He  by  His  grace  re- 
tained us  ;  we  should  be  let  in  the  race  set  before 
us,  so  as  never  to  attain,  unless  He  freed  us  from 
the  burden  of  our  sins.  "  He  who  willeth  and 
runneth  must  glory  not  in  himself,  but  in  Him

Author  of  merit,  Who  both  applies  our  will  to  the  work,  and  unfolds  th< 
work  to  our  will.  Else  if  we  would  speak  rightly  of  what  we  call  oui 
merits,  they  are  a  sort  of  seed-plot  of  hope,  incentives  of  love,  tokens 
of  the  hidden  predestination,  presages  of  future  bliss,  the  way  to  th< 
kingdom,  not  the  cause  of  reigning.  For  whom  He  justified,  not  whorr 
He  found  just,  them  He  glorified.''  S.  Bern,  de  lib.  arb.  fin.

from  Whom  he  had  both  to  will  and  to  run."  Let 
us  adore  and  thank  Him  Who  is  the  Way ;  let  us 
hold  on  in  the  way  ;  and  we  shall  see  that  we  have 
the  same  hope,  trust,  stay,  our  one  Lord  and  God, 
Who  is  above  all  to  protect,  and, through  all,  by 
His  power  and  working,  and  in  all  by  His  grace 
and  love. 

All  is  of  Christ.  His  is  the  grace,  which  brought 
us  out  of  the  mass  of  our  natural  corruption  in 
Adam.  His  was  the  new  principle  of  life,  which 
in  baptism  he  imparted  to  us.  His  the  grace  which 
cherished,  nurtured,  enlarged,  that  first  gift,  or  if 
unhappily  we  wasted  it,  through  repentance,  brought 
us  back,  converted,  renewed,  restored  us.  His,  each 
gift  of  superadded  grace,  whereby  He  rewards  the 
use  which,  through  His  grace,  we  make  of  each  former 
grace,  bestowing  grace  for  grace.  And  life  eternal, 
too,  will  be  from  Him,  grace  for  grace.  For,  as 
S.  Augustine  says,  "  If  our  good  life  is  nothing  else 
than  the  grace  of  God,  without  doubt  eternal  life, 
which  is  given  to  a  good  life,  is  the  grace  of  God ; 
for  it  too  is  given  gratis,  because  that  to  which  it 
is  given,  is  given  gratis.  But  that  to  which  it  is 
given,  is  merely  grace ;  but  this  which  is  given  to 
it,  since  it  is  its  reward,  is  grace  for  grace,  as  a 
reward  for  righteousness,  that  that  may  be  true, 
(since  it  is  true,)  that  God  shall  render  to  every 
man  according  to  his  works  f." 

f  De  Grat.  et  lib.  arb.,  c.  viii.  §  20.  t.  x.  p.  728.

But  although  faith  and  works  are  one  whole,  yea, 
"  the  one  work  in  which  all  works  are,  is  '  faith, 
which  worketh  by  love/  as  the  Lord  Himself  says, 
'  This  is  the  work  of  God,  that  ye  believe  in  Him 
whom  He  hath  sent8/  "  God  assigns  to  us  works 
as  the  test  of  our  faith,  not  faith  as  the  test  of  our 
works.  And  this,  because  it  is  easy  to  deceive  our- 
selves as  to  our  faith  or  our  feelings ;  it  is  not  so 
easy  to  deceive  ourselves  as  to  our  deeds,  if  we  will 
but  look  into  our  consciences  by  the  light  of  the 
law  of  God.  It  is  easy  to  say,  "  Lord,  Lord  ;"  it  is 
not  easy,  but  of  the  power  of  the  grace  of  God,  to 
"deny  ourselves  and  take  up  our  cross  and  follow 
Him."  It  is  a  toilless  task  to  "hear  His  words 
and  do  them  not,  building  a  house  upon  the  sand." 
It  is  not  easy  to  be  poor  in  spirit,  and  meek,  and 
pure  in  heart,  and  to  pray  without  ceasing,  and  in 
every  thing  to  give  thanks ;  to  resist  "  the  lust  of 
the  flesh,  and  the  lust  of  the  eye,  and  the  pride  of 
life,"  and  "  keep  thyself  unspotted  from  the  world." 
It  is  easy,  while  going  along  the  broad  way,  to  call 
up  to  one's-self,  out  of  some  forgotten  corner  of  the 
heart,  a  vague  belief  of  the  mercy  of  God  in  Christ 
Jesus.  It  is  not  easy,  amid  the  fire  of  passion 
within,  the  manifold  force  of  temptation  without, 
the  delusive  pleasures  dancing  before  our  eyes,  the 
treachery  of  our  own  hearts,  to  be  "  dead  to  the 
world,  that  we  may  live  to  God."  It  is  an  easy, 
costless,  confession,  to  own  ourselves  what  we  are, 

1  S.  Aug.  in  Ps.  Ixxxix.  fin. 


45 

*• 

"  unprofitable  servants ;"  it  is  hard,  first  to  labour 
with  our  whole  strength,  through  the  grace  of  God, 
to  "do  all  things  whatsoever  He  hath  commanded," 
and  then,  and  then  only,  it  will  be  the  fruit  of  God's 
grace  to  owrn  it. 

But  hard  though  it  be,  our  Lord,  if  ye  indeed 
seek  Him,  will,  by  His  grace,  make  it  easy.  For  He 
saith,  "  My  yoke  is  easy."  Meditate  but  a  little 
daily,  on  the  truths  of  faith.  Faith  will  open  to 
your  sight  heaven  and  your  eternal  home.  Faith 
will  shew  to  you  your  Lord  at  the  right  hand  of 
God  interceding  for  you,  locking  down  with  pity 
upon  you,  for  you  pleading  those  five  glorious 
wounds,  which,  radiant  with  the  glory  of  His  God- 
head, fill  heaven  with  adoring  amazement  at  the 
boundlessness  of  His  love  for  each  one  of  us.  Faith 
will  shew  you  the  vacant  throne,  amid  the  choirs  of 
angels,  vacant  for  each  of  you,  if  you  pray  for  the 
grace  of  Christ  to  persevere  unto  the  end.  Faith 
will  shew  you  the  serene  peace,  the  mutual  charity, 
the  adoring  love,  the  blissful  contemplation,  the 
transporting  gladness,  the  pure  harmony,  the  Divine 
beauty,  the  thrilling  joy  of  unutterable  thankfulness, 
the  unsating  fulness  of  bliss,  the  indissoluble  union 
with  thy  Redeemer  and  thy  God,  where  the  plea- 
sures at  His  Right  Hand  are  for  evermore. 

Then  embody  thy  faith  in  acts.  Faith  without 
acts  of  faith  is  but  a  dream.  If  thou  believest  that 
thy  Judge  in  the  Great  Day,  will  reward  deeds  of 
mercy,  and  punish  the  unmerciful,  deny  thyself 


46 

that  thou  mayest  shew  mercy  to  Him  in  His  poor. 
If  thou  believest  that  "the  pure  in  heart  shall  see 
God,"  pray  Him  Who  searcheth  the  heart,  to  cleanse 
thine,  and  admit  not  into  it  any  thought  which 
leads  to  sin.  If  thou  believest  that  "  the  world  pass- 
eth  away,"  set  not  thy  hopes,  thy  love,  thy  ambition, 
on  this  passing  world,  to  pass  away  with  the  world 
on  which  thou  buildest.  If  thou  believest  in  eter- 
nity, live  for  eternity.  Sow  sparingly,  if,  so  sowing, 
thou  hopest  to  reap  bountifully.  Sow  to  the  flesh, 
if,  so  sowing,  thou  hopest  to  reap  incorruption. 
"  Walk  in  the  ways  of  thy  heart,  and  in  the  sight 
of  thine  eyes,"  if  "for  these  things  God  will"  not 
"  bring  thee  into  judgment11."  But  if  thou  believe 
that  "  God  worketh  in  us  to  will  and  to  do  of  His 
good  pleasure,"  that  He  is  the  Author,  He  the 
Finisher,  He  the  exceeding  great  Reward  of  thy 
faith,  then,  what  thou  doest,  do,  not  for  the  praise 
of  men,  not  for  thine  own  exaltation,  not  for  any 
worldly  end,  but  for  God.  If  God  is  thine  end, 
then  see  how  thou  mayest  with  a  strong  hand,  by 
the  grace  of  God,  cast  forth  out  of  thyself  what 
may  displease  God ;  how  thou  mayest  perfect  in 
thyself,  by  His  grace,  any  grace  which  God  hath 
given  thee;  how  thou  mayest  by  strong  impor- 
tunity, besiege  the  love  of  God,  and  obtain  from 
Him  any  grace  thou  lackest. 

So  shalt  thou  find,  not  in  words  but  in  life,  that 
faith  and  deeds  of  faith   are  one,  given  in  one  by 

h  Eccles.  xi.  9. 


47 

God  to  thee,  and  from  thee  in  one  to  go  back  to  God. 
As  thou  by  faith  beholdest  tbe  greatness  of  God 
and  of  His  eternal  grace,  His  ineffable  holiness, 
majesty,  glory,  goodness,  love,  thou  wilt  know 
and  feel  the  nothingness  of  all  in  thyself,  whether 
faith  or  works,  save  as  they  are  the  gift  of  God. 
As  thou  probest  thyself,  thou  wilt  see  the  more 
thine  own  evil.  But  as  thou  ownest  thine  own  evil 
and  God's  good,  He  will  take  away  from  thee  thine 
evil,  and  crown  in  thee  His  own  good  ;  as  thou 
ownest  thyself  in  thyself  an  unprofitable  servant, 
He,  owning  in  thee  His  own  work,  will  say  unto 
thee,  "Well  done,  good  and  faithful  servant,  enter 
thou  into  the  joy  of  thy  Lord."  Amen.

S.  AUGUSTINE'S  HABMONY  OP  S.  PAUL  AND  S.  JAMES, 
ON  FAITH  AND  WOBKS. 


that  the   Apostle   Paul,   preaching  that    "a  man 
is  justified  by  faith  without  works,"  was  not  rightly  under- 
stood by  those,  who  so  understood  the  saying  as  to  think,  that 
when  once  they  had  believed  in  Christ,  they  could  be  saved  by 
faith,  although  they  did  evil  deeds  and  lived  wickedly :  this 
passage  of  his  Epistle  (S.  James  ii.  20.)  explains  that  same 
meaning  of  the  Apostle  Paul,  how  it   is  to   be  understood. 
Therefore  he  the  rather  uses  the  example  of  Abraham,  that 
faith  without  good  works  is  void ;  because  the  Apostle  Paul 
also  used  the  example  of  Abraham,  to   prove  that  "man  is 
justified  by  faith  without  the  deeds  of  the  law."     Eor  when  he 
commemorates  the  good  wrorks  of  Abraham  which  accompanied 
his  faith,  he  plainly  shews  that  the  Apostle  Paul  did  not  in 
such  wise  teach,  through  the  example  of  Abraham,  that  a  man 
is  justified  by  faith  without  works,  as  that  any  should  believe 
that  it  pertaineth  not  unto  him  to  do  good  works ;  but  this 
rather,  that  no  man  should  think  that,  by  the  merits  of  works 
gone  before,  he  had  attained  to  the  gift  of  justification  which  is 
by  faith.     Eor  herein  the  Jews  sought  to  set  themselves  above 
the  Gentiles  who  believed  in  Christ,  that  they  said  that  they 
had  attained  to  the  grace  of  the  Gospel  by  the  merits  of  good 
works  under  the  law :  and  thus  many  who,  from  among  them, 
had  believed,  were  scandalized,  that  the  grace  of  Christ  should 
be  given  to  the  uncircumcised  Gentiles.     "Wherefore  the  Apo- 
stle Paul  saith,  that  a  man  may  be  justified  by  faith,  without 
works,  but  those,  [works]  preceding  [faith.]     For  when  he  is 
justified  by  faith,  how  can  he  but  thenceforth  work  righteously, 
although  beforehand  having  wrought  nothing  righteously,  he 
attained  to  the  justification  of  faith,  not  by  the  merit  of  good 


49 

works,  but  by  the  grace  of  God,  which  cannot  now  be  void 
in  him,  since  now  he  "  worketh"  righteously  "  by  love."  But 
if  when  any  have  believed,  he  forthwith  depart ^  out  of  this 
life,  the  justification  of  faith  abideth  with  him ;  good  works 
neither  preceding  (because  he  attained  thereto  not  by  merit, 
but  by  grace,)  nor  following,  because  he  is  not  permitted  to 
remain  in  this  life.  Hence  it  is  manifest  that  what  the  Apo- 
stle Paul  saith ;  "  Therefore  we  conclude  that  a  man  is  justified 
by  faith  without  works,"  is  not  so  to'  be  understood  as  that,  if 
any  should  live  after  having  received  faith,  we  may  call  him 
righteous,  though  he  should  live  evilly.  Therefore  both  the 
Apostle  Paul  uses  the  example  of  Abraham,  because  he  was 
justified  by  faith  without  the  deeds  of  the  law  which  he  had 
not  received ;  and  the  Apostle  James  also,  because  he  proves 
that  good  works  followed  the  faith  of  Abraham  himself,  shew- 
ing how  what  the  Apostle  Paul  preached  is  to  be  understood. 

2.  For  they  who  think  that  this  saying  of  the  Apostle  James 
is  contrary  to  that  of  the  Apostle  Paul,  may  also  conclude  that 
even  S.  Paul  himself  contradicts  himself,  because  he  says  in 
another  place ;  "  For  not  the  hearers  of  the  law  are  just  before 
God,  but  the  doers  of  the  law  shall  be  justified."  (Rom.  ii.  13.) 
And  in  another:  "But  faith  which  worketh  by  love."  (GUI. 
v.  6.)  And  again :  "  For  if  ye  live  after  the  flesh,  ye  shall 
die ;  but  if  ye  through  the  Spirit  do  mortify  the  deeds  of  the 
flesh,  ye  shall  live."  (Kom.  viii.  13.)  What  those  deeds  of  the 
flesh  are,  which  are  to  be  mortified  through  the  deeds  of  the 
Spirit,  he  points  out  elsewhere,  saying :  "  Now  the  works  of 
the  flesh  are  manifest,  which  are  these :  adultery,  fornication, 
uncleanness,  lasciviousness,  idolatry,  witchcraft,  hatred,  vari- 
ance, emulations,  wrath,  strife,  seditions,  heresies,  envyings, 
murders,  drunkenness,  revellings,  and  such  like,  of  the  which 
I  tell  you  before,  as  I  have  also  foretold  you  in  time  past,  that 
they  which  do  such  things  shall  not  inherit  the  kingdom  of 
God."  (Gal.  v.  19—21.)  And  to  the  Corinthians  he  saith: 
"  Be  not  deceived :  neither  fornicators,  nor  idolaters,  nor  adul- 
terers, nor  effeminate,  nor  abusers  of  themselves  with  mankind, 
nor  thieves,  nor  covetous,  nor  drunkards,  nor  revilers,  nor  ex- 
tortioners, shall  inherit  the  kingdom  of  God.  And  such  were 
some  of  you ;  but  ye  were  washed,  but  ye  were  sanctified,  but 

<D 


50 

ye  were  justified  in  the  Name  of  the  Lord  Jesus,  and  by  the 
Spirit  of  our  God."  (1  Cor.  vi.  9 — 11.)  By  which  sayings  he 
most  plainly  teacheth,  that  they  had  not  attained  to  the  justi- 
fication of  faith  by  any  good  works  going  before ;  nor  had  that 
grace  been  given  to  their  deserts,  when  he  saith  :  "  And  such 
were  some  of  you."  But  when  he  saith  :  "  They  who  do  such 
things  shall  not  inherit  the  kingdom  of  God,"  he  plainly  shew- 
eth,  that  so  soon  as  they  believed,  they  ought  to  do  good  works. 
Which  also  S.  James  saith ;  and  in  many  places  altogether  the 
same  Apostle  Paul  preacheth  clearly  enough,  that  all  who  have 
believed  in  Christ  must  live  righteously,  lest  they  come  to 
punishment.  And  our  Lord  Himself  maketh  mention  of  the 
same  thing,  saying:  "Not  every  one  that  saith  unto  Me,  Lord, 
Lord,  shall  enter  into  the  kingdom  of  heaven,  but  he  that 
doeth  the  will  of  My  Father  which  is  in  heaven."  (Matt.  vii. 
21.)  And  elsewhere  :  "  Why  call  ye  Me  Lord,  Lord,  and  do  not 
the  things  which  I  say?"  (Luke  vi.  46.)  And:  "  Whosoever 
heareth  these  sayings  of  Mine,  and  doeth  them,  I  will  liken  him 
unto  a  wise  man,  who  built  his  house  upon  a  rock,  &c.  And  every 
one  that  heareth  these  sayings  of  Mine  and  doeth  them  not, 
shall  be  likened  unto  a  foolish  man,  who  built  his  house  upon  the 
sand,"  &c.  (S.  Matt,  vi,  24 — 7.)  Wherefore  the  sayings  of  the 
two  Apostles,  S.  Paul  and  S.  James,  are  not  contrary  the  one 
to  the  other,  when  the  one  saith  that  "  a  man  is  justified  by 
faith  without  works,"  and  the  other,  that  "  faith  without  works 
is  dead  ;"  because  S.  Paul  is  speaking  of  works  which  go  before 
faith,  S.  James  of  works  which  followed  after  faith :  as  also 
S.  Paul  himself  sheweth  in  many  places. — S.  Aug.  Quaestt.  83. 
q.  76.  t.  vi.  p.  67,  8.  ed.  Ben.

ADVERTISEMENT  TO  THE  THIRD  EDITION. 

THIS  Sermon  on  "  the  Rule  of  faith"  has  remained  long 
out  of  print ;  in  the  first  instance,  because  of  some  trouble 
in  verifying  the  quotations  1  from  Liguori's  "  Glories  of 
Mary/'  which  some  Roman  Catholic  controversialist  had 
impugned.  I  have  since  twice  verified  them  (having  lost 
the  first  verifications)  by  the  conscientious  Redemptorist 
edition,  published  with  the  imprimatur  of  two  successive 
Archbishops  and  Cardinals,  Archbishops  Wiseman  and 
Manning. 

Subsequently,  as  long  as  there  was  any  hope  that  com- 
munion might  be  restored,  yet  we  ourselves  remain  under 
our  own  Bishops  (which  the  martyred  Archbishop  of  Paris, 
Mgr.  Darboy,  said  to  me,  he  thought  might  well  be)  and 
so  that  we  should  not,  in  case  of  restored  communion,  be 
flooded  with  these  or  similar  devotions  to  the  Blessed 
Virgin,  there  seemed  to  be  no  longer  any  occasion  to  dwell 
upon  these  devotions,  which  have  always  been  our  special 
crux,  further  than  I  had,  in  my  first  Eirenicon,  shewn  that 
they  were  our  special  cmx,  and  how  keenly  we  felt  these 
innovations  of  the  later  Roman  system. 

The  whole  Roman  system  was  changed  by  the  Vatican 
Council.  Until  its  close,  the  rule  of  faith  at  least  was  the 
same.  The  Roman  Church  too  acknowledged  with  the 
Fathers,  that  the  sole  source  of  Faith  was  God's  revelation 
of  Himself  in  Holy  Scripture;  the  interpreter  of  Holy

iv     Faith  transmitted  every  where, preserved  every  where. 

Scripture  was  the  same,  the  universal  Church  from  the 
first,  according  to  the  saying,  "  quod  semper,  quod  ubique, 
quod  ab  omnibus."  The  same  body  of  truth,  which  was 
attested  by  Holy  Scripture,  was  taught  by  the  Apostles 
every  where,  before  a  word  of  Holy  Scripture  was  written. 
Believed  every  where,  it  was  transmitted  every  where. 
The  unlettered  martyrs  knew  it  better,  because  more 
simply,  than  some  of  the  learned,  whose  writings  may  have 
been  preserved  to  us.  There  have  been  doubts  about  the 
faith  of  single  writers,  counted  in  the  general  title  of  "  the 
fathers,"  and  valid  as  testimonies,  except  in  what  was  pe- 
culiar to  each, — Origen,  Tertullian  and  others.  Origen's 
writings  infected  even  S.  Gregory  of  Nyssa.  The  faith  of 
the  Church  remained  the  same.  This  was  brought  out  by 
General  Councils,  in  which  Bishops,  lettered  or  unlettered, 
were  assembled  from  all  parts  of  the  world.  All  attested, 
'  So  have  we  received  •'  and  the  concurrent  testimony  of 
all,  and  of  every  individual,  was  accepted  as  evident  proof 
of  a  common  original.  Heresy  enlarged  the  explanations 
of  the  Church :  it  did  not  develope  its  doctrine,  which 
was  the  same  before,  as  afterwards. 

The  Bishops  of  Rome  (as  they  were  then  called)  as  the 
only  Apostolic  See  of  the  West,  had,  of  course,  a  great 
share  in  this ;  but  it  was  only  a  share.  There  is  evidence 
of  their  gathering  the  judgements  of  Western  Bishops2,  m 
which  case  they  represented  the  whole  West.  At  the  Coun- 
cil of  Nice,  the  Bishop  of  Rome  certainly  did  not  preside  . 
at  the  first  Council  of  Constantinople,  one  only  Western 
Bishop  was  present,  and  he  in  no  relation  to  Rome.  The 
enlarged  Creed  of  Constantinople  (our  Nicene  Creed)  was 
framed  for  the  needs  of  the  Eastern  Church,  and  continued 
to  be  their  Creed  alone  for  70  years,  until  it  was  received 
by  the  whole  Church  at  the  Council  of  Chalcedon 3.

S.  Cyril  to  Nestorius,  in  which  Pope  Celestine  had  wholly 
concurred,  was  submitted  to  the  Council,  and  each  Bishop 
pronounced  his  own  individual  judgement  upon  it,  without 
deference  either  to  S.  Cyril  or  S.  Celestine;  the  Epistle  of 
Nestorius,  upon  which  S.  Celestine  had  condemned  him, 
was  considered  and  condemned  by  an  independent  judge- 
ment, and  Nestorius  himself.  In  a  letter  to  that  Council, 
S.  Celestine  speaks  of  the  whole  Council  as  inspired  by  God 
the  Holy  Ghost  in  a  way  which  he  does  not  claim  singly 
for  himself. 

At  the  Council  of  Chalcedon5  the  tome  of  S.Leo  was  read; 
expressions  were  doubted  about  by  some  Bishops  of  Illyria 
and  Palestine,  but  were  accepted,  on  the  ground  of  like 
expressions  of  S.  Cyril  of  Alexandria:  finally  the  whole 
was  accepted,  not  because  it  emanated  from  the  Bishop  of 
Rome,  but  because  it  agreed  with  the  General  Councils 
which  had  preceded  it.  The  Roman  legates  themselves 
describe  the  Council  of  Ephesus  by  the  words  "  the  exposi- 
tion of  which  Creed,  set  forth  at  Ephesus  by  Cyril  of  blessed 
memory."  The  Bishops  in  a  long  succession,  one  by  one, 
expressed  their  concurrence  with  it  on  the  ground  of  that 
agreement.  S.  Leo  spoke  of  the  strength  which  the  faith, 
which  he  had  himself  put  forth,  had  gained  through  the 
concurrence  of  the  600  Bishops  of  the  Council. 

The  fifth  General  Council  had  the  account  of  the  proceed- 
ings of  the  Council  of  Ephesus  in  regard  to  the  Epistles  of 
S.  Cyril,  Nestorius,  and  Celestine,  recited  to  them,  and  the 
approval  of  S.  Leo's  Epistle  to  Flavian  in  the  Council  of 
Chalcedon  and  adopted  their  proceedings  as  a  guide  to  their 
own.  But  the  special  subject  of  their  praise  was  that  the 
Council  did  not  accept  the  writings  without  examination : 

"6  From  the  aforesaid  it  has  become  manifest  how  the  holy 
synods  have  been  wont  to  approve  what  is  brought  before 
them.  For  although  those  most  holy  men  who  wrote  the

tinguished  [splenduerunt] ,  yet  the  Synod  did  not  approve 
those  Epistles  simply  and  without  examination,  unless  they 
had  ascertained  that  they  were  in  all  things  consonant  with 
the  exposition  and  doctrine  of  the  holy  fathers,  with  which

uttered  one  harmonious  word." 

"Following  then  this  rule/'  they  had  the  decree  of 
Chalcedon  read,  as  the  test  whether  the  writings  of  Ibas, 
Theodorus,  and  those  alleged  of  Theodoret,  agreed  with  it. 

The  independent  examination  of  the  writings  of  even 
eminent  Popes  by  General  Councils,  in  order  to  ascertain 
their  agreement  with  the  faith  laid  down  by  previous  Coun- 
cils, which  had  taken  place  in  the  third  or  fourth  General 
Councils,  was  laid  down  as  a  principle  in  the  fifth. 

S.  Gregory  the  Great  in  an  Encyclical  letter  to  all  the 
Patriarchs,  professes,  ' ' 7  I  receive  and  venerate  the  four 
Councils  as  I  do  the  four  holy  Gospels.  The  fifth  Council  I 
venerate  in  like  way.  All  the  persons  whom  the  venerable 
Councils  aforesaid  reject,  I  reject ;  those  whom  they  reve- 
rence, I  receive ;  because,  seeing  they  are  established  by 
universal  consent^  whoever  presumes  either  to  loose  whom 
they  bind  or  to  bind  whom  they  loose,  destroys  himself,  not 
them." 

This  is  not  the  language  of  one  who  might  himself  have 
written  the  decrees  of  those  Councils,  and  whose  single 
voice  would  have  saved  all  the  toil  and  sacrifice  of  life  in- 
volved in  the  gathering  of  aged  Bishops  from  all  quarters 
of  the  world.  Had  Papal  infallibility  been  then  believed, 
Sylvester  or  S.  Damasus  or  S.  Celestine  or  S.  Leo  might  by 
themselves  have  set  to  rest  the  heresies  of  Arius  or  Mace- 
donius  or  Nestorius  or  Eutyches. 

Pope  Vigilius  in  his  second  "  Constitutum"  recognises 
that  the  Council  of  Chalcedon  only  accepted  the  Epistle  of 
S.Leo  after  ascertaining  that  it  agreed  with  the  three 
general  Councils  before  it,  and  says  that  it  required  this.

Fifth  and  sixth  General  Councils.  vii 

He  recites  from  the  Acts  the  allegations  of  the  Bishops,  that 
S.  Leo's  Epistle  agreed  with  the  preceding  Councils,  and 
that  they  therefore  received  it;  then  says,  "8  These  things 
being  so,  no  one  doubts  that  our  fathers  did  believe  that  the 
Epistle  of  the  Blessed  Leo  was  on  that  ground  received 
by  them,  that  it  agreed  with  the  doctrines  of  the  Synods  of 
Nice  and  Constantinople,  as  also  with  those  of  the  Blessed 
Cyril  set  forth  in  the  first  Council  of  Ephesus."  He  then 
argues,  "  If  then  that  Epistle  of  so  great  a  Pontiff,  reful- 
gent with  such  light  of  orthodox  faith,  requires  (exigit)  to 
be  approved  by  such  comparison ;  how  could  that  Epistle 
to  Maris  be  supposed  to  be  called  orthodox  by  the  same 
fathers,  &c. 

In  the  sixth  General  Council  the  dogmatic  letters  of  Pope 
Agatho,  and  of  the  Roman  Council  held  by  him,  were  pro- 
posed for  acceptance.  The  Patriarch  and  the  Bishops 
asked  for  copies  of  both,  in  order  to  compare  them,  and 
the  authorities  alleged  in  them,  with  the  MSS.  in  the  Pa- 
triarchal Library9.  This  being  granted,  in  the  next  Session, 
three  weeks  afterwards,  the  same  question  was  asked.  The 
Patriarch  answered,  al  Having  inspected  the  whole  bearing 
of  the  relations  sent  by  Agatho,  the  most  holy  Pope  of  the 
elder  Rome,  and  from  his  Synod,  and  having  diligently 
searched  the  books  of  the  holy  and  approved  fathers,  laid 
up  in  my  Patriarchate,  I  found  all  the  testimonies  of  the 
holy  and  approved  fathers  contained  in  those  relations 
agreeing  and  in  nothing  differing  therefrom,  and  I  agree 
therewith,  and  so  I  confess  and  believe."  Another  Bishop 
said,  "  Having  heard  the  relations  sent  by  Agatho  the  most 
holy  Pope  of  Rome  to  our  good  lord,  I  have  found  that 
they  in  no  way  contradict  the  holy  fathers  and  I  confess 
two  wills,  &c."  Another  says  that  he  "had  read  them,  taken 
knowledge  of  the  testimonies  lying  in  them,  and  so  held ; 
for  so  he  had  believed  before,  when  they  were  read,  and 
still  believed."

Pope  Simplicius,  who  is  said  to  have  used  great  prudence 
in  writing  to  the  Emperor  Zeno  in  difficult  times,  joins  the 
authority  of  the  Church  with  his  own.  The  Vatican  de- 
cree says,  "  not  from  the  consent  of  the  Church."  Pope 
Simplicius  says,  "  with/'  He  says7,  "  What  has  deserved 
to  be  cut  off  with  the  edge  of  the  Gospel  pruning-hook  by 
Apostolic  hands,  with  the  assent  of  the  universal  Chicrch, 
cannot  recover  power  of  fresh  growth."  To  Acacius,  Pa- 
triarch of  Constantinople,  he  speaks  of  "  Timothy  the  Cat " 
as  a  threatening  new  conventions  for  himself,  thinking 
that  that  can  be  loosed,  which  the  authority  of  the  whole 
has  decreed  concerning  him."  He  says  that  "  a  Synod  was 
never  called,  except  when  some  new  perversion  arose,  or 
some  ambiguity  in  asserting  doctrine,  that,  if  there  was 
any  ambiguity,  the  authority  of  Episcopal  deliberation 
might  illumine  it,  when  they  treated  of  it  together,  as  the 
impiety  first  of  Arius,  then  of  Nestorius,  then  of  Dioscorus 
and  Eutyches  compelled  to  be  done."  The  authority,  which 
Simplicius  thought  it  "  abominable  "  to  contravene  in  act, 
was  not  his  own,  but  "  the  judgement  of  all  the  priests  of 
the  Lord  in  all  the  world." 

S.  Leo  III.  said  to  the  legates  of  Charlemagne,  "  9Far  be

Council  of  Chalcedon),  when  he  was  asked  to  admit  the 
Filioque  into  the  Creed.

Bossuet  adduces,  as  another  class  of  evidence,  how  in 
the  early  Church  questions,  upon  which  the  Bishop  of  Rome 
had  pronounced  in  the  strongest  way,  remained  unsettled 
until  a  General  Council.  There  can  hardly  be  a  more  pro- 
nounced way  of  speaking  ex  cathedra  on  any  matter  of 
faith  or  practice  than  to  excommunicate  or  renounce  the 
Communion  of  those  who  held  otherwise.

xii  Question  of  Easter  and  heretical  Baptism. 

Several  local  Councils 2  were  held,  from  which  it  appears 
that  the  Asiatic  mode  of  keeping  Easter  was  exceptional. 
Whether  communion  was  restored  or  no  3,  the  question  it- 
self remained  unsettled  till  the  General  Council  of  Nice, 
which,  without  censure  or  any  reference  to  previous  autho- 
rity, prescribed  one  uniform  mode  of  keeping  it.  "4The 
Syrians,  Cilicians  and  Mesopotamians  were,"  at  the  time  of 
the  council  of  Nice,  "  out  of  order  in  celebrating  the  Feast 
and  kept  Easter  with  the  Jews.  This  gave  occasion  for 
an  Ecumenical  Council,  that  the  feast  might  be  everywhere 
celebrated  on  one  day,  &c.  It  took  place  then  and  the 
Syrians  submitted.  They  [the  Council]  wrote  concerning 
the  Easter,  '  It  seemed  good  as  follows/  for  it  did  then 
seem  good  that  there  should  be  a  general  compliance." 
The  Asiatic  Churches,  which  had  disregarded  the  judge- 
ment of  the  Bishop  of  Rome,  submitted  to  the  Council. 

2.  In  the  early  Church  there  were  conflicting  opinions 
on  the  value  of  heretical  Baptism.  The  East  seems  mostly 
to  have  denied  or  doubted  its  validity 5 :  the  West,  to  have 
believed  that  it  was  valid,  if  the  Scriptural  words  were 
used,  although  the  Minister  who  used  them  (if  an  Arian) 
disbelieved  them.  In  Asia  Minor  the  denial  seems  to  have 
been  extended  to  schismatical  Baptism.  S.  Cyprian  and  a 
large  Synod  of  African  Bishops  affirmed  its  invalidity  : 
Stephen,  Bishop  of  Rome,  thereupon  renounced  his  com- 
munion. S.  Cyprian  wrote  to  S.  Firmilian,  a  very  eminent 
Bishop  in  Asia  Minor,  whose  answer  is  so  strongly  worded 
that  a  few  Roman  critics  have  questioned  its  genuineness. 
He  speaks  of  S.  Stephen  as  excommunicating  himself  when 
he  excommunicated  all  besides.

A  successor  of  Pope  Stephen  7  probably  restored  commu- 
nion with  S.  Cyprian.  There  is  no  evidence  that  S.  Cyprian 
retracted  anything.  S.  Augustine  praises  him  that  he  made 
no  schism.  Holding  him  to  be  in  error,  he  says,  "8We 
ourselves  should  not  venture  to  assert  anything  of  this

were  supported  by  the  most  concordant  authority  of  the 
Universal  Church;  to  which  he  himself  [S.  Cyprian]  would 
doubtless  yield,  if  at  that  time  the  truth  of  this  question  had 
already  been  solidly  established,  having  been  cleared  and 
declared  by  a  plenary  Council." 

A  "  plenary  Council "  then,  not  the  Bishop  of  Home, 
was,  in  S.  Augustine's  mind,  the  ultimate  authority.

the  judgement  of  the  "  plenary  Council  to  which  the  cause 
was  then  referred."  " 9  See,  let  us  suppose  that  all  the

xiv      Wrong  judgements  of  Popes  corrected  by  Councils, 

in  which  the  cause  might  be  canvassed  with  the  judges 
themselves;  so  that  if  they  should  be  proved  to  have

Afterwards  also  a  wrong  or  rash  decision  of  the  Bishop 
of  Rome  was  not  acquiesced  in.  When  Liberius  renounced 
the  communion  of  S.  Athanasius,  S.  Athanasius  only  gently 
lamented  his  fall.  When  Cselestius  appealed  to  Rome 
against  the  decision  of  African  Bishops  and  presented  to 
Zosimus  an  heretical  confession  of  faith,  Zosimus  in  error 
formally  acquitted  him.  He  spoke  of  his  confession  as  a 
"  good  confession,"  a  "  clear  and  open  statement ;"  of  his 
examination  as  to  "the  complete  faith  of  Caelestius;"  and 
censured  the  African  Bishops  for  not  believing  his  former 
memorial ;  he  wished  the  African  Bishops  to  retract  their 
judgement  "  for  the  better,"  said  that  his  accusers  would 
have  to  prove  that  Caelestius  thought  otherwise  than  he  had 
put  down  in  his  memorial  and  confession.  An  African  Coun- 
cil of  214  Bishops  shewed  him  that  Pelagius  and  Caelestius, 
whom  he  had  acquitted,  had  been  condemned  by  Innocent 
his  predecessor :  and  spoke  of  his  approving  that  memorial 
as  Catholic  being  liable  to  be  mischievous  unless  corrected1.

xvi    Unanimous  consent  of  Church  against  Adoptianism. 

(monks)  was  recited  and  refuted  and  Justinian's  profession

The  lawfulness  of  an  expression,  touching  the  Holy 
Trinity,  was  settled,  not  by  the  Bishop  of  Rome  to  whom 
appeal  was  made,  but,  after  he  had  cast  a  slur  upon  it,  by 
the  most  eminent  Theologian  of  the  time,  to  whom  appeal 
was  made  subsequently. 

In  later  times  also  the  unanimous  judgement  of  the 
Church  was  thought  necessary  to  establish  a  matter  of 
faith.  When  the  heresy  of  Adoptianism  broke  out  in  Spain, 
Charlemagne  enquired  by  letter1,  "What  thought  the 
Apostolic  Lord  with  the  holy  Koman  Church  and  the 
Bishops  dwelling  in  those  parts;  2)  What  the  Bishop  of 
Milan  thought  and  the  doctors  and  priests  of  the  Churches 
of  Christ  in  Italy;  3)  what  those  of  Germany,  Gaul  and 
Aquitaine."  Adrian  anathematised  Elipand  and  his  followers. 
Yet  this  was  not  enough.  Charlemagne,  in  harmony  with 
Adrian  who  sent  two  legates,  assembled  the  great  Council 
of  Frankfort.  This  condemned  the  patent  heresy.  From 
it  Charlemagne  wrote  to  Elipand  and  his  fellow-bishops  in 
Spain,  professing  for  himself  that  he  "  held  the  Catholic 
faith,  delivered  by  Apostolic  teachers,  and  preserved  by  the 
whole  Church : "  he  says,  that  he  ' '  had  gathered  a  Council 
from  all  the  Churches  of  his  realm,  in  order  that  the  holy 
unanimity  of  all  might  decree  firmly  what  was  to  be  be- 
lieved as  to  the  adoption  of  the  flesh  of  Christ ;  "  that  he 
had  written  to  the  pontiff  of  the  Apostolic  see,  wishing  to 
know  what  the  holy  Roman  Church,  taught  by  Apostolic 
traditions,  would  answer;"  that  he  had  "called  some  from 
Britain."  Of  all  alike  he  urged  the  " 2  pious  unanimity  and 
peaceful  investigation  : "  "  the  faith  strengthened  by  the 
testimony  of  many,"  "  the  authority  of  the  Apostolic  see 
and  the  Episcopal  unanimity." 

Charlemagne,  though  a  layman,  is  a  competent  witness 
of  what  was  thought  necessary  to  the  force  of  a  decree  on 
matters  of  faith — the  unanimous  consent  of  the  Church.

Decretals  contradict  Papal  Infallibility.          xvii 

This  is  plainly  the  direct  contradictory  of  the  Vatican 
decree,  that  the  Pope  is  infallible  "  not  by  consent  of  the 
Church."  Yet  Popes  sought  this  confirmation. 

" 2  The  judgement  of  a  general  Council  never  was  recon- 
sidered but  was  obeyed.  It  was  a  saying  of  S.  Gelasius 
an  excellent  Pontiff,  ( 3  A  good  and  Christian  synod,  once 
passed,  cannot  and  ought  not  to  be  discredited  by  any  re- 
iteration of  a  new  Synod/  The  judgement  of  the  Holy 
Spirit  is  discredited,  whenever  it  is  reconsidered  by  a  new 
judgement.  But  a  judgement  propounded  by  a  Roman 
Pontiff  is  of  such  sort  that  it  was  reconsidered  by  a  new 
judgement.  It  was  not  then  that  last  and  ultimate  judge- 
ment of  the  Church." 

Even  in  the  12th  century,  Pope  Eugenius  III.  approved 
of  the  Decretals,  and  commanded  them  to  be  read  in  the 
universities,  although  they  set  the  orbis  terrarum  above 
the  Pope,  and  directly  asserted  his  fallibility  in  matters  of 
faith.

xviii  Council  of  Constance  above  the  Popes. 

those  Sanctions  or  decretal  Epistles  in  which  nothing  is 
found  contrary  to  the  decrees  of  preceding  fathers  or  the 
precepts  of  the  Gospel/' 

The  objects  for  which  the  Council  of  Constance  was  as- 
sembled forced  upon  it  a  question  which,,  except  in  a  dis- 
eased state  of  things,  could  never  occur ;  whether  a  Council 
was  superior  to  a  Pope  or  a  Pope  to  a  Council.  For  both  a 
Council  as  the  representative  of  the  whole  Church,  and  the 
Bishop  of  Eome  as  having  from  old  times  a  Primacy  in  it, 
ought  to  be  of  one  mind.  Being  called  together,  as  the 
last  resource  to  end  the  long  schism  between  the  Popes  at 
Rome  and  at  Avignon,  the  Council  had  to  decide  between 
the  claims  of  three  anti-popes  or,  if  necessary,  to  obtain 
the  resignation  of  all.  It  was  therefore,  by  its  office,  supe- 
rior to  all. 

The  anti-popes,  whose  cession  it  had  to  obtain,  were  each 
of  them  a  disgrace  to  the  Papacy.  The  worst  was  John 
XXIII.,  whose  name  stands  in  the  list  of  Bishops  of 
Home,  who  had  convened  the  Council,  and  who  fled  from 
it  when  the  list  of  crimes  imputed  to  him,  some  of  which 
he  owned  and  some  denied,  was  privately  circulated.  We 
naturally  cannot  think  much  of  a  Council  which  induced 
the  Emperor  Sigismund  to  break  his  safe-conduct  to  Huss. 
The  Council,  however,  gave  rise  to  the  subsequent  discus- 
sions as  to  the  superiority  of  a  Council  to  the  Pope.  It 
said,  " 1  This  holy  Synod  of  Constance,  being  lawfully 
called  together  in  the  Holy  Spirit,  constituting  a  General 
Council  and  representing  the  Catholic  Church,  has  its 
power  immediately  from  Christ,  and  every  one,  of  whatever 
state  or  dignity,  even  if  it  be  Papal,  is  bound  to  obey  it  in 
what  appertains  to  the  Faith  and  to  the  extirpation  of  the 
said  schism  and  the  reformation  of  the  said  Church  in  its 
head  and  its  members/'  It  also  enacted,  "  that  if  any  one 
of  any  condition,  state,  dignity  whatever,  even  if  Papal, 
should  contumaciously  refuse  to  obey  the  precepts  of  this 

1  Cone.  Const.  Sess.  v. 


Canonists  against  Papal  Infallibility.  xix 

sacred  Synod  or  any  other  General  Council  soever  lawfully 
called,  he  should  be  subjected  to  condign  penitence  unless 
he  repented,  and  should  be  duly  punished  even  by  recourse 
to  other  aids  of  law  if  need  be." 

The  discussion  as  to  the  relative  superiority  of  a  Council 
or  a  Pope  lasted  long.  With  regard  to  individuals,  it  is 
remarkable  that  those  who  held  the  Pope  to  be  superior 
to  the  Synod  did  not  hold  his  infallibility.  I  will  give  the 
summary  in  the  words  of  a  Roman  Catholic  writer  before 
the  Council2: 

"3Panormitan,  f4the  light  of  the  law/  his  master  Car- 
dinal Zabarella,  Cardinal  Cusa,  Alphonsus  Tostato,  (5the 
amazement  of  the  world/  nor  less  '  distinguished  for  holi- 
ness/ his  countryman  Alphonsus  de  Castro,  and  Pope 
Adrian  VI.  (not  to  mention  many  other  great  names), 
have  left  writings  hostile  to  the  view  of  papal  infallibility. 
All  this  is  admitted  by  Ultramontane  controversialists 
of  the  sixteenth  century,  before  Bossuet  was  born.  But 
the  most  extreme  partisans  of  the  papacy,  those  who 
asserted  the  papal  infallibility  in  the  strongest  terms, 
really  held  it  as  little  as  the  most  determined  Gallicans. 
Turrecremata  certainly  teaches  that  the  'judgement  of  the 
Roman  pontiff  cannot  err  in  those  things  which  are  of 
faith/  But  this  is  only  one  side  of  his  teaching.  Another 
and  not  less  important  side  of  that  teaching  is,  that  a  pope 
may  be  convicted  of  pertinacity  in  heresy,  'si  err  or  em  definit 
solenniter  et  a  Christianis  asserit  tanquarn  Catholicum  esse 
tenendum.'  He  reconciles  the  two  propositions  by  a  third, 
namely,  that  if  a  Roman  pontiff  becomes  a  heretic,  by  the 
very  fact,  through  which  he  falls  from  the  faith  of  Peter, 
he  falls  from  the  chair  and  See  of  Peter,  and  consequently 
the  judgement  of  such  a  heretic  would  not  be  the  judge-

xxii  Pope  Honorius. 

with  the  Church.  "  1  Changing  the  constitution,"  said  a 
French  Bishop  during  the  Council,  "  you  are  obliged  to 
change  also  the  doctrine,  and  it  will  be  necessary  hereafter 
to  chant  in  the  Holy  Sacrifice  Credo  Papam  instead  of

Facts  went  the  same  way.  The  case  of  Honorius  alone 
was  spoken  of  in  the  Council.  It  was  evidently  felt  as  a 
sore  point.  It  was  got  over  in  the  old  way  of  alleged  fal- 
sification of  documents.  The  expedient  that  he  did  not 
speak  ex  cathedra,  did  not  occur  to  any  one.  This  would 
have  been  to  admit  the  error.  It  was  also  too  contrary  to 
facts.  The  letter  of  Sergius,  the  heretical  patriarch  of 
Constantinople,  to  Honorius,  as  well  as  those  which  he 
wrote  to  Cyrus  or  Sophronius,  and  the  letter  of  Honorius  to 
him,  were  spoken  of  by  the  YIth  General  Council  as  dog- 
matic writings.  Sergius  in  his  letter  to  Honorius  set  down 
his  own  belief  written  with  great  care,  and  set  forth  how 
Cyrus  Patriarch  of  Alexandria  had  won  back  to  the  Church 
many  Eutychians  by  proposing  to  them,  —  in  fact,  Monothe- 
lisna;  how  Sophronius  had  remonstrated  against  this,  speak- 
ing of  two  operations  in  Christ  ;  how  he  himself  had  ex- 
horted Cyrus  "  not  to  allow  any  one  to  speak  of  one  or  two 
operations  in  Christ  our  God/'  seeing  that  the  word  "  two 
operations"  scandalised  many,  and  that  to  speak  of  "  two 
wills"  suggested  the  thought  of  two  contrary  human  wills 
[not  of  a  Divine  and  Human  Will]  .  This  he  laid  before 
Honorius,  entreating  him  to  read  it  carefully  and  in  his  love, 
according  to  the  grace  given  him  "  by  God,  to  fill  up  any 
deficiency,  and  through  your  holy  syllables  to  signify  2  what 
seems  good  to  you  as  to  these  matters  8." 

Sophronius  Patriarch  of  Jerusalem,  being  himself  de- 
tained by  the  irruption  of  the  Saracens,  sent  Bishop  Stephen 
to  Rome,  having  solemnly  adjured  him  to  "make  known  to 
the  most  holy  man  all  the  commotions  here  [in  the  East] 
and  to  give  them  no  rest  until  they  canonically  effect  an

On  the  other  hand,  the  usual  resource  in  perplexity,  the 
imputation  of  interpolation,  is  absolutely  precluded  by 
the  independence  of  the  authorities  6.  The  imputation  of 
heresy  is  attested  by  Pope  Leo  II.  in  accepting  the  sixth 
General  Council  and  in  Epistles  to  the  Spanish  Bishops 
and  the  Spanish  king ;  by  another  Pope  in  his  Profession 
of  faith  on  entering  his  office ;  by  Pope  Adrian  II.,  to 
justify  the  condemnation  of  Honorius;  by  the  seventh  and 
eighth  General  Councils  (of  which  the  eighth  was  entirely 
under  Roman  influence) ;  by  the  framers  of  the  Roman  Bre- 
viary before  its  revise  by  Pius  V.  and  Clement  VIII.  Had 
Honorius  not  been  guilty,  this  had  been  a  prolonged  false 
witness  of  about  900  years  7.

Vacillations  of  Pope  Vigilius.  xxv 

8.  Nicholas  I.  gave  as  a  response  to  the  infant  Church  of 
the  Bulgarians,  that  Baptism  in  the  name  of  Christ  alone 
was  sufficient7. 

9.  Alexander  III.  declared  that  he  judges  contrary  to 
some  of  his  predecessors  in  a  question  of  marriage  8. 

The  fall  of  Liberius  was  different  from  these.  It  was  a 
terrible  fall.  He  knew  and  held  the  truth,  but  denied  it. 
He  strengthened,  not  his  brethren,  but  those  who  denied 
his  Lord.  But  it  was  as  Bishop  of  Rome,  that  his  assent 
was  desired  and  his  agreement  with  the  Arians  obtained ; 
as  Bishop  of  Rome,  he  signed  the  heretical  Creed,  rejected 
the  communion  of  S.  Athanasius,  and  professed  himself 
at  peace  and  in  concord  with  the  worst  enemies  of  the  faith. 
"Anathema  to  thee,  thou  prevaricator  Liberius,"  burst 
forth  S.  Hilary  in  relating  his  sad  history  9. 

The  case  of  Sergius  was  again  different.  He  had  pur- 
chased the  Papacy  and  obtained  a  large  sum  of  money 
(700  pounds  of  gold)  on  condition  that  he  would  abrogate 
the  Council  of  Chalcedon  and  receive  into  communion 
some  of  the  Monophysite  heretics  (the  Acephali).  He  pro- 
mised part  of  his  bribe  (200  pounds  of  gold)  to  Belisarius, 
on  condition  that  he  would  remove  Sylverius  and  make  him 
Pope  in  his  stead;  Belisarius,  having  at  first  banished 
Sylverius,  gave  him  into  the  hands  of  Sergius,  who  removed 
him  to  the  Isle  of  Palmaria,  where  he  died  of  starvation 
and  was  held  to  be  a  martyr.  Sergius,  bound  by  his  pro- 
mise, wrote  privately  to  the  heads  of  the  Acephali,  declar- 
ing that  he  held  the  same  faith  with  them ;  and  in  his 
confession  of  faith,  which  he  begged  them  to  keep  secret, 
declared  himself  a  Monophysite,  anathematised  those  who 
held  the  two  natures  in  Christ,  and  rejected  the  Epistle  of 
S.Leo  which  the  Council  of  Chalcedon  had  received. 
Publicly  he  accepted  what  privately  he  had  rejected1. 

In  him  we  have  only  the  vacillations  of  one  who  had 
been  a  bad  man.     He  wished  to  hold  with  the  Westerns

This  as  authoritative  as  things  now  held  infallible,  xxvii 

6  weeks  after  this,  Vigilius  in  a  laboured  writing,  which 
also  he  called  "  Constitutum,"  by  an  artificial  train  of  rea-

These  judgements  were  all  formal  judgements,  as  their 
names  "  Judicatum,"  "  Constitutum,"  imply.  Yet  they 
contradicted  one  another;  Vigilius  justified  himself  by 
the  example  of  S.  Augustine,  who  "  4  reconsidered  his  own 
writings  and  corrected  his  sayings/5  and  said, ' ( 5  by  the  de- 
finition of  this  our  present  writing  we  evacuate  whatever 
has  been  done  either  by  me  or  by  others  in  defence  of  the 
three  chapters  aforesaid/' 

Pelagius  II.  justified  the  variation  on  the  ground,  that 
the  change  of  one  seeking  the  truth  is  not  to  be  blamed. 
" 6  If  in  the  matter  of  the  3  chapters  one  thing  was  said 
when  truth  was  being  sought,  another  when  truth  was 
found,  why  is  change  of  judgement  imputed  as  a  fault  to 
this  See,  which  is  reverenced  in  its  author  by  the  whole 
Church  ?  For  not  change  of  judgement,  but  inconstancy 
of  mind  is  matter  of  blame.  When  then  the  intention  of 
seeking  what  is  right  remains  unchanged,  why  should  one 
not,  quitting  his  ignorance,  change  his  language?"

xxxiv  Establishment  of  the  Faith,  office  of  the  Church. 

history  of  the  Church  would  have  been  other.  Almighty 
God  did  not  will  that  it  should  be  by  the  voice  of  one  man, 
that  heresies  should  be  slain.  He  had  an  office  for  the  Uni- 
versal Church  spread  throughout  the  world.  He  had  an 
office  for  the  Church  as  a  whole,  to  bear  witness  to  the 
truth.  One  voice  went  up  from  every  clime,  "  So  have  we 
been  taught ;"  "  Thus  believes  the  Catholic  Church ;"  " l  and 
thereupon  they  confessed  how  the  faith  lay,  in  order  to 
shew  that  their  own  sentiments  were  not  novel,  but  Apos- 
tolical ;  and  what  they  wrote  down,  was  no  discovery  of 
theirs,  but  is  the  same  as  was  taught  by  the  Apostles." 

The  Council  of  Nice  was  a  wonderful  assembly.  "  2  There 
were  at  that  time,  many,  eminent  for  Apostolic  gifts ;  many 
top,  who,  according  to  the  Divine  Apostle,  '  bore  about  in 
the  body  the  marks,  of  the  Lord  Jesus/  James  of  Nisibis 
bpth  raised  the  dead  to  life,  and  did  very  many  other  mira- 
cles. Paul  B,isliop  of  Neo-caesarea  had  experienced  the  fury 
of  Licinius,  his  hands  powerless,  the  red-hot  iron  had  destroy- 
ed the  power  of  motion;  others  had  their  right  eyes  dug  out, 
others  were  hamstrung  in  the  knees,  of  whom  was  Paphnu- 
tius.  A  crowd  of  martyrs  niight  be  seen  gathered  in  one." 

But  all  the  Bishops,  however  endowed,  learned  or  un- 
learned, knew  the  faith  of  Christ.  And  the  faith,  which  they 
attested,  surmounted  every  shqck ;  the  violence  of  Roman 
or  Persian  Emperors,  of  Gothic  or  Vandal  kings,  or  the 
wiles  of  heretics,  or  gatherings  pf  heretical  Bishops,  be- 
cause it  was  builded  on  the  Rock  which  was  Christ.  Petrus 
super  petram,  non  petra  super  Petrum.  The  faith  in  Christ, 
Son  of  God  and,  for  us,  Son  of  man,  was  the  Rock,  against 
which  the  gates  of  heU  should  not  prevail. 

So  it  was  with  the  subsequent  Councils.  The  Councils 
knew  nothing  of  the  infallibility  of  Popes  :  the  Popes,  re- 
presented in  them,  knew  nothing  of  it :  the  Popes,  who 
regarded  the  acceptance  of  their  letters  by  Councils  as 
a  confirmation  of  them,  knew  no.thing  of  it ;  nor  those 
who  retracted  what  they  had  said  and  owned  their  falli- 
bility; nor  the  Church,  when  in  successive  Councils  it

to  carry  the  decree  at  any  cost,  and  the  minority,  at  one 
time  very  considerable,  melted  away,  and  retired  mostly 
from  the  Council,  some  almost  broken-hearted.  "  To  what 
end  to  struggle  against  one  stronger  than  one's  self  ?" 
said  Mgr.  Darboy 3,  who  went,  unknowing,  to  die  by  the 
hands  of  those,  whom  the  Church  had  lost  and  who  became

The  Vatican  decree  revives  much  which  had  passed 
away>  and  whose  revival  the  English  Roman  Catholics,  60 
years  ago,  did  not  think  possible.  "  The  Pope's  claim  to 
temporal  power  by  Divine  right,"  says  C.  Butler 1,  "  has 
not  perhaps  at  this  time  a  single  advocate."  It  is  now 
with  Roman  Catholics  infallible  truth,  having  been  de- 
clared in  a  Papal  Bull,  and  acted  upon  in  the  depositions  of 
Henry  VIII.  and  of  Elizabeth.  And  in  detail,  it  is  infalli- 
ble truth,  that  the  Pope  has  a  right  to  depose  any  Prince, 
to  require  subjects  to  renounce  their  obedience,  to  rise  in 
arms  against  him  and  drive  him  from  his  kingdom,  to  re- 
quire all  princes,  in  the  virtue  of  holy  obedience,  to  make 
war  against  him,  empowering  all  to  take  as  slaves  any 
born  in  his  dominions  whoever  they  might  be,  and  to  seize 
their  property  as  their  own2.  Some  at  the  Council  ap-

against,  on  the  ground  that  the  book,  from  which  it  was 
cited,  had  been  placed  in  the  Index.  Twelve  passages 
only  were  cited  from  that  book,  and  of  these  one  only 
does  not  occur  in  other  writers.  Why  therefore,  it  was 
so  placed,  I  know  not.  But  it  is  useless  to  repeat  any  of 
this  evidence  now,  since  the  chief  of  it  has  been  made  to 
Roman  Catholics  infallible  truth. 

All  the  comparisons,  which  so  startled  and  distressed  us, 
between  the  love  of  Mary  and  Jesus,  have  to  Roman  Ca- 
tholics now  received  their  adequate  explanation,  but  in  the 
sense  contrary  to  what  we  hoped.  Since  the  Council  of 
Trent  only  laid  down,  that  c  it  is  good  and  useful  to  pray 
to  the  saints/  we  thought  that  such  sayings,  as  I  have  here 
and  elsewhere  dwelt  upon,  were  no  part  of  the  faith  of  the 
Roman  Communion,  and  that  therefore  we  need  not  con- 
cern ourselves  with  them,  except  to  say  that  they  were  to 
us  the  main  hindrance  to  restored  communion.  We  could 
not  except  to  any  degree  of  love  to  her,  whom  our  Re- 
deemer loves  with  such  special  infinite  love,  whom  in  all 
eternity  He  fore-elected  to  be  His  mother.  Our  exception 
was  not  to  the  love,  or  to  her  intercession  :  still  less,  could 
we  presume  to  wish  or  think  of  limiting  in  thought  the 
love  of  such  a  Mother  and  the  Son  Who  vouchsafed  to 
take  His  flesh  from  her.  What  we  excepted  against  was  the 
office,  popularly  assigned  to  her,  of  the  Mediatrix  with  the 
Only  Mediator  revealed  to  us  in  Holy  Scripture  or  known  to 
the  Universal  Church  of  old,  our  Lord  and  our  God,  Who 
bids  us  come  to  Him,  if  we  are  weary  and  heavy  laden. 
He  did  not  bid  us  to  go  to  His  .Mother,  rather  than  Him- 
self. The  words  cannot  be  softened.  When  S.  Alphonso

Effects  of  foiled  decretals.  xlv 

Bull  of  the  Immaculate  Conception  and  the  Encyclical  of  last 
year  will  mark  an  epoch  in  the  re-constitution  of  the  Chris-* 
tian  order  of  the  world. }>  The  Pope  is,  according  to  him, 
to  be  continually  declaring  new  matters  of  faith,  to  be  be- 
lieved, without  authority  of  Scripture  or  tradition,  on  his 
sole  authority,  or  supposed  to  have  authority  of  Scripture 
or  tradition,  solely  because  he  declares  them. 

One  special  misery  of  this  new  dogma  of  "  Infallibility  " 
is  that  it  is,  to  such  an  extent,  grounded  on  forgery.  Of 
old  no  one  doubted  the  genuineness  of  the  forged  decre^ 
tals  :  now,  no  one  defends  them.  They  were  first  alleged 
by  Hincmar  about  A.D.  860  in.  behalf  of  his  own  metropo-^ 
litan  rights :  they  were  employed  against  him  in  the  foU 
lowing  year  by  Pope  Nicholas  I.  It  is  difficult  ta  imagine 
how  a  Bishop  of  Rome,  not  without  learning,  could  have 
thought  them  to  be  genuine,  since  there  could  have  been 
in  the  papal  archives  no  vestige  of  the  long  unbroken 
series  of  letters  or  of  decrees  of  Councils  which  they  em- 
bodied. The  Roman  Catholic  historian  Pleuri  has  detailed 
at  length  the  change  which  they  made  in  the  relations 
of  Rome  to  the  Western  Churches 8.  A  thousand  years 
passed  before  they  have  had  their  full  effect ;  but,  without 
the  forged  Decretals,,  the  Papal  Infallibility  never  could 
have  become  a  doctrine  of  the  Roman  Communion., 

It  is  a  childlike  state  of  mind  to  believe  everything  ppo.- 
posed  to  belief,  because  it  is  proposed.  But  it  is  a  great 
strain  on  belief,  that,  because  any  one  be  chosen  as  Bishop 
of  Rome,  whatever  his  antecedents,  sins,  crimes,  he  is,  at 
once,  a  god  upon  earth,  the  Vicar  of  Jesus  Christ,  whereas 
some  of  the  Popes  of  the  middle  ages  were  more  like  the 
heathen  gods,  Jupiter  or  Mars,  than  images  of  the  Living 
God.  Whether  these  claims  will  prepare  for  the  Coming  of 
Christ,  or,  by  their  oppressiveness  on  belief,  of  His  last  anta- 
gonist, the  Anti-Christ,  God,  the  Omniscient,  only  knows.

the  order  of  proceeding.  The  Protest  sets  forth  that, 

"  In  the  General  Congregation  of  the  Vatican  Council,  April  29,  their  Eminences,

Disregard  of  minority  of  Vat.  C.  by  its  majority,  xlvii 

was  to  be  abandoned,  and  that  the  first  subject  to  be  treated  of  was  Chapter  XI 
of  that  scheme,  and  the  decree  added  to  it,  i.  e.  of  the  infallibility  of  the  Roman 
Pontiff,  separately  and  apart  from  the  connection  between  the  rights  and  preroga- 
tives of  the  Primacy  with  other  doctrines  as  to  the  Church." 

It  was  not,  in  fact,  a  mere  question  of  order  but  of  the  substitu- 
tion of  the  personal  and  sole  infallibility  of  the  Pope  for  the  iner- 
rancy of  the  Church,  viz.  that  our  Lord,  by  His  promises  that  He 
would  be  with  His  Apostles  and  their  successors  to  the  end  of  the 
world,  and  that  the  gates  of  hell  should  not  prevail  against  His 
Church,  guaranteed  that  the  whole  Church  should  not  fall  into  error, 
destructive  of  His  truth. 

'2  According  to  the  original  scheme,'  (those  Bishops  say),  *  proposed 
on  March  6th,  it  was  to  be  defined  that  the  infallibility  of  the  Roman 
Pontiff  relates  to  the  same  object  as  the  infallibility  of  the  Church.' 
Their  plea  then  was,  that,  '\vithout  a  manifest  disturbance  of  the 
logical  order,  this  object  [of  the  infallibility  of  the  Roman  Pontiff] 
could  not  be  denned,  unless  the  subject  of  the  Church,  and  the  ob- 
ject to  which  the  infallibility  of  the  Church  extends,  were  first 
treated  of.' 

The  result  of  this  change  of  order  was,  that  the  Church  was  ex- 
cluded altogether  from  having  any  part  in  the  doctrine  of  2  infalli- 
bility thenceforth  to  be  held  de  fide.  But  foi?  this  change,  the 
office  of  the  Church  throughout  the  world  in  preserving  the  faith 
against  any  emerging  heresies  must  have  been  first  laid  down :  as  it 
was,  that  office,  in  the  form  of  the.  Decree  ultimately  adopted,  was 
altogether  denied  as  a  heresy3.  The  Church  thenceforth  is  simply  a 
recipient  of  what  the  Roman  Pontiff  authoritatively  promulgate. 

The  sixty-seven  Bishops  probably  foresaw  that  issue.  They  pro- 
test against  it,  beforehand,  because  they  had  found  petitions  useless.

They  conclude, 

"  4  It  suffices  us  to  have  set  forth  this  our  persuasion,  without  adding  any  petition. 
For  we  can  no  longer  reconcile  it  with  our  Episcopal  dignity,  with  the  office  which 
we  have  in  this  Council,  with  the  rights  appertaining  to  us  as  members  of  the 
Council,  to  present  petitions.  We  have  already  been  taught  superabundantly  by  ex- 
perience, that,  so  far  from  such  petitions  being  regarded,  they  are  not  thought  worthy 
pf  an  answer.  The  only  thing  then  left  to  us,  is  to  express  our  dissent  and  protest 
against  this  mode  of  proceeding,  which  we  hold  to  be  most  pernicious  to  the  Church 
and  the  Holy  Apostolic  See,  that,  so  far  as  relates  to  ourselves,  we  may  thus  escape 
having  to  give  account  for  the  unhappy  consequences,  which  doubtless  will  shortly 
arise  and  are  already  arising  therefrom,  both  with  man  and  in  the  aweful  judgement 
of  God  :  whereof  be  these  very  letters  a  lasting  memorial." 

This «  account,'  they  say,  *  will  have  to  be  given  by  those  who  do  not 
employ  this  Council  to  provide  for  urgent  necessities  of  the  Christian 
Church,  who,  overcoming,  not  the  enemies  of  the  Church,  but  their 
brethren,  and  gaining  the  victory  for  opinions  of  the  schools,  will 
inflict  the  gravest  injury  on  the  Church:  which,  considering  the  cir- 
cumstances of  the  Church  now,  and  still  more  in  the  future,  is  matter 
of  continued  fear  and  anguish.' 

This  inverted  order  of  proceedings  was  aggravated  by  the  fact 
that  the  infallibility  of  the  Roman  Pontiff  was  not  mentioned  among 
the  grounds  of  convening  the  Council.  The  Bishops  say, 

"  5  When  first  the  declaration  of  Papal  infallibility  was  asked  for  in  a  public 
paper  published  at  Rome,  all  tbe  enemies  of  the  Church  cried  out— and  the  un- 
godly language  spread  more  and  more  throughout  the  world— that  the  holy  Father 
had  convoked  the  Bishops  to  Rome  under  plea  of  the  public  good,  but,  in  truth, 
only  to  increase  his  own  power,  and  so  out  of  an  unworthy  motive ;  that  the  grounds 
given  in  the  Bull  of  June  19th  1868  for  convoking  an  (Ecumenical  Council  were  to 
be  of  no  account,  viz.  that  a  Council  should  be  gathered,  that  by  the  counsels  of  the 
whole  Episcopate,  it  might  be  weighed  with  exactest  care,  what  healthful  reme- 
dies there  might  be  for  the  calamities  of  our  times,  to  promote  the  glory  of  God, 
the  salvation  of  souls,  the  instruction  of  Christian  youth,  the  common  peace  and 
concord  of  all."

the  Church,  in  which,  by  God's  Providence,  they 
have  been  placed.  There  is  a  yet  more  subtle  peril, 
by  which  some  elsewhere  have  been  tempted,  and 
others  have  fallen,  the  peril  of  accustoming  them- 
selves to  take  up  with  a  state  of  uncertainty  as  to

making  shipwreck  of  the  faith  altogether. 

The  source  of  faith  is,  beyond  doubt,  the  Holy 
Scriptures.  The  language  of  S.  Leo  and  S.  Augus- 
tine is  the  same  as  that  of  our  Articles.  "  They," 
says  S.  Leoa,  "are  not  to  be  accounted  Catholics, 
who  do  not  follow  the  definitions  of  the  venerable 
Synod  of  Nice,  or  the  rules  of  the  holy  Council 
of  Chalcedon,  inasmuch  as  it  is  plain  that  the  holy 
decrees  of  both  issue  from  the  fountain  of  the 
Gospels  and  Apostles."  And  when  the  vision  of 
S.  Perpetua,  which  has  since  been  alleged  in  proof 
of  Purgatory,  was  alleged  to  S.  Augustine  in  proof 
that  Baptism  was  not  needed  for  the  remission  of 
original  sin,  he  answered  "  that b  writing  is  not  in 
that  canon  of  Scriptures,  whence  testimonies  are  to 
be  produced  in  questions  of  this  sort."  S.  Jerome's

Such  is  the  proceeding  of  all  the  great  Councils  on 
the  Faith ;  such,  of  its  individual  defenders,  alike 
of  S.  Irenaeus f,  Clement  of  Alexandria  or  Origen ; 
Tertullian,  S.  Cyprian,  S.  Augustine  or  S.  Optatus ; 
S.  Athanasius,  S.  Hilary  or  the  S.  Gregories ;  S.  Basil 
or  S.  Ambrose,  S.  Chrysostom  or  S.  Epiphanius  or 
S.  Jerome ;  Theophilus  of  Alexandria  or  S.  Cyril, 
or  Theodoret.  To  use  the  words  of  ones,  "  all 
things  that  are  delivered  to  us  by  the  Law,  Prophets, 
and  Apostles,  we  receive,  and  know,  and  acknow- 
ledge, looking  for  nothing  more  than  these.  For  it 
is  impossible  we  should  speak,  or  so  much  as  think 
any  thing  of  God,  besides  those  things  which  are 
divinely  told  us  by  the  divine  oracles  both  of  the 
Old  and  New  Testament.7'

4  The  rule  of  faith  as  maintained 

received,  and  for  which,  more  than  all  besides,  the 
Church  is  indebted  to  him  unto  the  end  of  time. 
Supporting  it  by  the  testimonies  of  the  fathers  before 
himh,  he  himself  says  of  it,  "  whatsoever1  was  written 
in  it,  is  proved  to  have  been  taken  from  the  autho- 
rity of  the  Apostles  and  Evangelists."  The  neglect 
of  this  he  alleges  as  a  ground  of  heresy :  "  they  k  fall 
into  this  phrenzy,  when  being,  through  some  obscu- 
rity which  they  meet  with,  hindered  from  knowing 
the  truth,  they  betake  themselves,  not  to  the  voices 
of  the  Prophets,  not  to  the  writings  of  the  Apos- 
tles, not  to  the  authority  of  the  Gospels,  but  to  them- 
selves ;  and  therefore  become  manifestly  teachers 
of  error,  because  they  became  not  disciples  of  the 
truth." 

We  acknowledge  that  Holy  Scripture  is  the 
source  of  all  saving  truth ;  but  it  does  not  therefore 
follow  that  every  one,  unguided,  is  to  draw  for  him- 
self the  truth  out  of  that  living  well.  The  Sixth 
Article  lays  down  the  duty  of  the  Church,  as  the 
groundwork  of  every  subsequent  statement  of  doc- 
trine. It  says  nothing  of  any  right  or  duty  of  every 
or  any  individual  to  satisfy  himself  that  every  article 
of  the  Creed  can  be  so  proved,  much  less  of  any 
liberty  of  any  one  to  reject  what  he  cannot  so  provre. 
It  is  often  the  very  condition  of  retaining  faith  alto- 
gether, to  continue,  even  for  a  long  time,  to  believe 
without  seeing ;  even  if,  with  all  the  diligence  which 
a  person  can  use,  he  cannot  see  the  proof  of  an  arti- 
cle of  faith.  This,  especially  with  the  young,  will  be

the  point  of  divergence,  of  -which  one  side  will  end 
in  a  perfect  intelligent  belief,  the  other,  in  total 
unbelief.  Such  rejection  of  one  point  has  ended  in 
atheism.  For  it  was  the  resistance  to  the  grace  of 
God,  and  trust  in  self.  The  very  existence  of  Creeds, 
side  by  side  with  Holy  Scripture, — summaries  of  its 
teaching,  yet  not  identical  with  it;  capable  of  being 
proved  by  it,  but  received  before  it  and  independent 
of  it ;  made  ours  in  Baptism,  when  we  were  uncon- 
scious; rehearsed  in  our  names,  as  our  belief;  taught 
without  doubt  or  faltering  as  the  truth  of  God,  as 
much  as  the  Holy  Scriptures  themselves ;  inworked 
into  our  spirit  by  devotion;  day  by  day  made  part  of 
our  very  being  by  being  spoken  to  Almighty  God  as 
our  faith, — shews  that  we  were  not  meant  ourselves 
to  have  any  choice  as  to  our  faith.  And  this  is  apart 
from  the  very  aweful  sentences,  with  which  the  Atha- 
nasian  Creed  is  fenced,  that  we  "hold,"  i.  e.  retain 
faithfully,  "the  Catholic  Faith'7  which  we  have  once 
received.  The  very  name,  "  the  Catholic l  Faith," 
"  the  Catholio  religion,"  "  the  Christian  verity,"  by 
"  which  we  are  compelled  to  acknowledge  "  what  is 
in  accordance  with  it,  and  "forbidden  to  say"  what 
is  contrary  to  it,  shews  at  once,  that  in  the  belief  of 
our  Church  which  has  received  this  Creed,  at  least 
the  whole  doctrine  of  the  Trinity,  the  Incarnation, 
the  Person  of  our  Eedeemer,  as  well  as  the  rest  of 
the  Apostles'  Creed,  everlasting  rewards  and  ever- 
lasting woe,  are  to  be  believed  very  exactly,  without

it  is  necessary  that  he  hold  the  Catholic  Faith.  And  the  Catholic 
Faith  is  this, — Like  as  we  are  compelled  by  the  Christian  verity — 
so  we  are  forbidden  by  the  Catholic  religion."
